findings.statement: The system's intended use — analysing applicants' CVs and recorded video interviews and scoring them so recruiters can prioritise candidates — falls under Annex III point 4(a) as a system used to analyse and filter job applications and evaluate candidates, and is therefore high-risk under Article 6(2); because the scoring profiles natural persons, the Article 6(3) derogation cannot remove that classification.

The AI Act requirements relevant to this deployment are in application: deployer obligations for Annex III high-risk systems apply from 2 August 2026 under Article 113(2), and the Article 4 AI-literacy duty and the Article 5 prohibitions have applied since 2 February 2025 under Article 113(3)(a).

The company uses the system under its authority and is therefore a deployer within the meaning of Article 3(4) of the AI Act, and, as the body determining the purposes and means of screening applicants, it is the controller under GDPR Article 4(7).

Scoring applicants from their CVs and video interviews is automated processing that uses personal data to evaluate personal aspects relating to the applicants, in particular their suitability and performance at work, and therefore constitutes profiling within the meaning of GDPR Article 4(4).

Before and while using the system, the company must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure it is used in accordance with the provider's instructions for use and must assign human oversight of the system to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, authority and support — in this scenario the recruiters who act on the scores.

Because the company feeds the system with the CVs and video recordings it has collected, it exercises control over input data and must ensure that data is relevant and sufficiently representative in view of the system's intended purpose.

During use the company must monitor the system's operation on the basis of the instructions for use, inform the provider and, where relevant, the market surveillance authority of risks and serious incidents, suspend use where the system may present such risks, and keep the logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent under its control, for at least six months unless Union personal-data law provides otherwise.
Before putting the system into service or using it at the workplace, the company as employer must inform workers' representatives and the affected workers that they will be subject to its use.
Since the system makes or assists in making decisions about the applicants, the company must inform each applicant that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system.
The company must take measures, to its best extent, to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among its staff, including the recruiters who operate the system and act on its scores.

The recorded video interviews are analysed in a recruitment context, which is within the workplace area where the AI Act prohibits placing on the market, putting into service and using AI systems to infer emotions of natural persons except for medical or safety reasons; to the extent the scoring infers applicants' emotions, that use is prohibited.

The scores are used to prioritise candidates for interview invitations, which affects applicants' access to employment; a decision based solely on such automated processing is subject to the data subject's right not to be subject to it under GDPR Article 22(1), unless an Article 22(2) exception applies, and where the contract or explicit-consent exceptions are relied on the company must implement Article 22(3) safeguards, at least human intervention, the right to express a point of view and to contest the decision.

Before using the system the company must carry out a data protection impact assessment: the scoring is a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing including profiling, on which decisions affecting applicants are based, and the AI Act further requires the company to use the information the provider supplies under its Article 13 for that assessment.

When collecting CVs and video interviews the company must inform applicants of the existence of automated decision-making, including profiling referred to in GDPR Article 22(1) and (4), and provide at least meaningful information about the logic involved as well as the significance and envisaged consequences of the scoring for them.

Applicants subject to a decision taken by the company on the basis of the system's output, which they consider to adversely affect their fundamental rights (for example, not being prioritised for interview), have the right to obtain from the company clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision.

summaries.relevance: The single provision that pins the classification: it lists exactly this use case — systems used to analyse and filter job applications and evaluate candidates — so the entire chain of high-risk deployer duties for the recruitment scoring turns on it.
Brings Annex III systems into the high-risk category, which is what attaches the Article 26 deployer obligations and the Article 86 explanation right to the company's use.
Would allow de-classification of Annex III systems, but its final subparagraph keeps profiling systems high-risk, so the applicant-scoring tool cannot escape the high-risk regime.

Supplies the GDPR definition of profiling that the scoring of applicants from CVs and videos satisfies; it underpins both the AI Act's Article 6(3) no-derogation point and the Article 22 and Article 35 triggers.
Fixes the date from which the Annex III high-risk deployer obligations bind, establishing that the requirements are live when the company plans this deployment.
Fixes the earlier application dates for the Article 4 literacy duty and the Article 5 prohibitions, so those rules also bind before any use.
Definitional anchor for the company's deployer status, which is what attaches the Article 26 obligations to it.
Definitional anchor for the company's controller status, which is what attaches the GDPR duties cited to it.
The core pre-use and in-use duty to operate the high-risk system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use, framing every concrete measure the company must take before using the tool.
Places the human-oversight assignment on the company and identifies recruiters as the persons who must be equipped with competence, training, authority and support to oversee the scores.
Obliges the company, which controls the CV and video inputs, to police the relevance and representativeness of the data it feeds the system.
Imposes continuous monitoring, information of the provider and authorities, and suspension duties during the deployment of the scoring system.
Sets the six-month minimum logging duty, preserving the record of how the system scored candidates for later accountability.
The employment-specific pre-use information duty toward workers' representatives and affected workers, directly applicable to this workplace deployment.
Requires telling the applicants themselves that they are subject to the system, the AI Act's own transparency layer on top of the GDPR notice.
Bridges the two regimes by requiring the company to use the provider's Article 13 information when performing the GDPR Article 35 impact assessment.
Adds a standing duty to build AI literacy among the staff who operate the system and act on its outputs.

The only flat prohibition the scenario risks touching: it bans emotion inference in the workplace area, so the nature of the video-interview analysis determines whether the whole use is lawful at all.
Gives adversely affected applicants a direct right against the company to an explanation of the system's role in the decision and its main elements.
The central data-protection limit on the scoring pipeline, forbidding solely automated decisions with significant effects such as interview prioritisation of candidates.
The only gateways — contract necessity, legal authorisation, explicit consent — under which such automated decisions could lawfully proceed.
The safeguards — human intervention, expression of views, contesting the decision — the company must implement whenever it relies on those gateways.
The general prior-assessment duty that this processing triggers, making the DPIA a precondition of deploying the system.
The specific trigger — systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects through automated profiling on which decisions rest — that makes the DPIA mandatory for this recruitment scoring.
Requires telling applicants at collection about the automated scoring and providing meaningful information about its logic, significance and envisaged consequences.

actions: Verify whether the video-analysis component infers applicants' emotions, which would trigger the flat prohibition in AI Act Article 5(1)(f) in this workplace-area use.

Determine whether interview-prioritisation decisions rest solely on the automated scores or on meaningful human review, to settle the application of GDPR Article 22(1) and the adequacy of the oversight assigned under AI Act Article 26(2).

Establish who developed and placed the system on the market, and whether the company substantially modifies it or changes its intended purpose, which would make the company a provider under AI Act Articles 3(3) and 25(1).

Verify whether the CV and video processing involves biometric or other special categories of data under GDPR Article 9(1), since that affects the Article 22(4) limits and the content of the Article 35 assessment.

Verify the company's place of establishment or Union nexus for AI Act Article 2(1) and GDPR Article 3, and whether it is a financial entity within DORA Article 2(1), since the scenario states neither.
